explanation: Brilliant! EBP is a sweet spot that combines what science proves, what your clinical skills tell you, and what the patient actually prefers.

question: A patient gets too full during meals and leaves food untouched. What strategy should the nurse suggest?

options.A: Drink two large glasses of water immediately before eating
options.B: Wait until evening and consume the entire day's food at once
options.C: Eat small, frequent meals and snacks throughout the day
options.D: Stop eating all solid foods and rely strictly on clear broths

explanation: Grazing on smaller, nutrient-dense meals every few hours prevents early fullness and helps patients hit their daily calorie goals easily. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T009#GNS227_U6_T009_h6)

question: Why might a breastfeeding mother be given a progestin-only pill instead of a combined pill?

options.A: Minipills taste better for the baby
options.B: Estrogen can decrease the breast milk supply
options.C: Progestin stops milk production completely
options.D: Combined pills cause infant colic

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Estrogen in combined pills can negatively affect milk production, so we prefer progestin-only options (minipills) to keep breastfeeding going strong.

question: How does Staphylococcus aureus usually contaminate prepared foods like egg salads?

options.A: Prolonged exposure to direct sunlight
options.B: Direct handling by an infected food preparer
options.C: Absorption from contaminated soil during growth
options.D: Cross-contamination from raw root vegetables

explanation: Staph bacteria live naturally on our skin. If a food handler doesn't wash up well, the bacteria can easily transfer straight into the food during prep.

question: Why can traditional power dynamics sometimes delay medical care for pregnant women?

options.A: Women are legally banned from talking to doctors first.
options.B: Hospitals refuse to treat women without a signed consent form.
options.C: Men always prefer traditional herbs over modern medicine.
options.D: The woman may need to wait for the man's approval and funds.

explanation: When getting care depends entirely on someone else's permission and money, emergencies can worsen while waiting.

question: Why does the Model for Improvement focus on small tests of change rather than massive overhauls?

options.A: Hospital management bans large projects due to budget constraints
options.B: Small tests reduce risk and let staff see if a change works before spreading it
options.C: Regulatory bodies only permit one minor change per year
options.D: Patients refuse to participate in large-scale hospital studies

explanation: Spot on! Testing things on a small scale lets nurses safely try out new ideas without disrupting the whole ward.

question: If a patient holds onto too much carbon dioxide because they aren't breathing deeply enough, what acid-base imbalance happens?

options.A: Respiratory alkalosis
options.B: Respiratory acidosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis
options.D: Metabolic alkalosis

explanation: Well done! Carbon dioxide acts like an acid in the body. If it builds up in the lungs, the blood becomes too acidic—hence respiratory acidosis.

question: A patient with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is most likely to show which group of signs?

options.A: High male hormone levels, failure to release eggs regularly, and insulin resistance
options.B: Heavy bleeding, low blood pressure, and severe weight loss
options.C: Complete absence of pubic hair and early menopause
options.D: Frequent fever, pelvic pain, and purulent vaginal discharge

explanation: PCOS is a very common hormonal condition. It usually involves high levels of androgens (male hormones), irregular ovulation, and trouble handling insulin properly.

question: Which group of mental health conditions features overwhelming fear and ongoing distress?

options.A: Depressive and Bipolar Disorders
options.B: Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders
options.C: Anxiety and Trauma-Related Disorders
options.D: Personality Disorders

explanation: These disorders are tied to persistent fear, constant high alert, and stress linked to difficult life events. Keep building that clinical vocabulary!

question: A pregnant patient asks how to reduce dark patches on her face. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Scrub the face vigorously with harsh soap twice a day
options.B: Stop drinking milk immediately to clear skin pigment
options.C: Apply strong bleaching creams prescribed over the counter
options.D: Apply daily sunscreen and wear wide-brimmed hats outdoors

explanation: Sunlight makes facial darkening (melasma) pop out more. Advising sun protection is a simple, effective tip every nursing student should know!

question: A patient with long fallopian tubes presents with sharp pelvic pain and spotting early in pregnancy. What is the main condition to suspect?

options.A: Uterine fibroid degeneration
options.B: Normal intrauterine twin pregnancy
options.C: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
options.D: Ectopic pregnancy

explanation: When an egg takes too long to travel, it can implant inside the tube instead of the uterus. This is called an ectopic pregnancy and needs quick medical attention. You are learning fast!

question: A primary health clinic in a rural Nigerian community wants to improve antenatal care attendance. What is the best first step based on local health system realities?

options.A: Report all pregnant women who miss clinic dates to the police
options.B: Consult village development committees and local women leaders
options.C: Close the clinic until pregnant women start coming on their own
options.D: Wait for federal funds to build a brand new modern hospital

explanation: Engaging trusted local structures helps identify why women are not attending and builds culturally acceptable solutions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h3)

question: How does boosting a patient's understanding of food directly help their health?

options.A: It cures all existing vitamin deficiencies overnight
options.B: It stops the body from absorbing excess dietary fats
options.C: It empowers them to make healthier food choices on their own
options.D: It eliminates the need to ever consult a doctor again

explanation: Exactly! When patients truly understand the 'why' behind good food, they are much happier to change their habits willingly, without you standing over them.

question: You draw up an injection, but an emergency pulls you away before you can give it. What is the safest action?

options.A: Discard the prepared injection safely according to policy
options.B: Place the loaded syringe back inside the original multi-dose vial
options.C: Ask the next shift nurse to give the injection later on
options.D: Leave the syringe labeled clearly on top of the medication cart

explanation: An unattended, drawn-up medication is unsafe because its safety and sterility can no longer be guaranteed. When in doubt, discard it safely and start fresh.

question: Why might a baby born to a mother with sickle cell disease grow more slowly in the womb?

options.A: Excessive amounts of amniotic fluid crushing the developing baby
options.B: Direct genetic damage to the fetal brain by maternal white cells
options.C: Reduced oxygen and nutrient transfer through the placenta
options.D: Premature closure of the fetal heart valves during the second trimester

explanation: Well done! When sickle cells slow down blood flow in the placenta, the baby gets less oxygen and food, which can slow down growth.

question: What is the main goal of food hygiene and safety practices?

options.A: To ensure food is safe and wholesome for consumption
options.B: To make meals taste better and look colorful
options.C: To make cooking faster in large kitchens
options.D: To cut down the cost of buying ingredients

explanation: Food hygiene is all about stopping contamination so the food we eat stays safe and healthy from the farm or market straight to the table!

question: Why do nurses sometimes use alternative checks like arm span or knee height for elderly patients instead of a standing height?

options.A: Spinal curvature and frailty make accurate standing height difficult
options.B: Elderly patients prefer sitting down during clinical examinations
options.C: Skinfold calipers cannot open wide enough on aged skin
options.D: Standard scales are unable to register weights below fifty kilograms

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like kyphosis (bent spine) make standing straight on a stadiometer nearly impossible, so arm span saves the day.

question: When local nurses aren't paid well and move abroad for better opportunities, what is this workforce loss called?

options.A: Resource rationing
options.B: Capital budgeting
options.C: Brain drain
options.D: Market inflation

explanation: Well done! 'Brain drain' describes when skilled professionals leave their home country seeking greener pastures, which really hits our local health sector hard.

question: What is the main job of synovial fluid inside a joint?

options.A: To supply blood vessels directly to the articular cartilage
options.B: To anchor skeletal muscles directly to the bone
options.C: To reduce friction and nourish the cartilage
options.D: To produce white blood cells during an infection

explanation: Spot on! Because cartilage doesn't have its own blood supply, synovial fluid acts like engine oil—bringing nutrients and keeping movements smooth.

question: Why does stopping your antibiotics halfway through cause drug resistance?

options.A: It forces the body to produce too many white blood cells
options.B: It makes the remaining tablets expire much faster in storage
options.C: It allows the strongest bacteria to survive, mutate, and multiply
options.D: It immediately cures the viral infection causing the fever

explanation: Exactly! Stopping early kills only the weak germs, leaving the tough, stubborn bacteria alive to multiply and become resistant to future drugs.

question: What is the main purpose of giving medications to clients with inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: To prevent family members from developing the same condition
options.B: To completely repair the damaged DNA inside the cells
options.C: To relieve specific symptoms and improve day-to-day comfort
options.D: To permanently stop the natural progression of the disease

explanation: Medications target troubling symptoms like spasms, pain, and stiffness to make the client more comfortable. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T15#GNS222_U4_T15_h4)

question: What term describes the heavy emotional stress and guilt a health worker feels after being involved in a patient safety incident?

options.A: Second victim syndrome
options.B: Professional burnout
options.C: Post-traumatic stress disorder
options.D: Compassion fatigue

explanation: It sounds heavy, but 'second victim syndrome' is very real. Clinicians who experience a tragic accident often need a lot of support and compassion too.

question: What is the primary role of nutrition in clinical nursing care?

options.A: Lowering hospital cleaning costs
options.B: Replacing the need for routine medications
options.C: Accelerating nursing shift handovers
options.D: Serving as a therapeutic tool for healing

explanation: Food and proper nutrition provide the essential building blocks the body needs to repair tissues and fight off disease, making it a key part of medical treatment. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T001#GNS227_U2_T001_h1)

question: During a mental check, which sign is most typical for a patient with moderate to severe anxiety?

options.A: Flat affect and delayed motor movements
options.B: Delusions of grandeur and unresponsiveness
options.C: Profound lethargy and deep sleepiness
options.D: Rapid speech and poor ability to concentrate

explanation: When anxiety is high, the brain is racing! Patients often talk fast, jump between thoughts, and find it really hard to focus on questions.

question: Why do emergency planners insist that temporary latrines must be built downhill and far away from community water sources?

options.A: To ensure the smell blows away from the tents
options.B: To prevent sewage from contaminating the community's drinking water supply
options.C: To keep the ground dry and prevent mud
options.D: To make them easier to clean with heavy machinery

explanation: Gravity makes liquid flow downhill. If toilets are uphill from wells or streams, waste will wash straight into the drinking water. Basic hygiene logic!

question: What is the main danger of a cytokine storm in severe COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.B: Severe tissue damage from a hyperactive immune response
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of taste and smell
options.D: Complete shut down of bone marrow white blood cell production

explanation: A cytokine storm happens when the immune system goes into overdrive, flooding the lungs with chemicals that end up harming healthy tissue. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: What do we call learning to fear something simply by watching how other people react to it?

options.A: Reading a medical textbook about anxiety
options.B: Developing a fear directly from a physical injury
options.C: Learning to fear something by watching others react with fear
options.D: Inheriting a phobia gene from a grandparent

explanation: This is observational learning! If a child sees a parent scream at the sight of a lizard, the child might pick up that exact same fear just by watching.

question: What is the main legal purpose of a patient's nursing care record?

options.A: A temporary shift handover note
options.B: A permanent legal record of care
options.C: A statistical data collection tool
options.D: A personal journal for the nurse

explanation: Great job thinking like a professional! Your notes aren't just paperwork—they stand as official legal proof in court and hospital reviews of the care you gave.

question: Which animal vector transmits the parasite that causes malaria?

options.A: Female Anopheles mosquito
options.B: Domestic housefly
options.C: Freshwater blackfly
options.D: Multimammate rat

explanation: Malaria parasites are transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h3)

question: A patient starts having a psychomotor seizure while sitting on a chair in the ward. What should you do immediately?

options.A: Force a padded tongue depressor firmly between the teeth
options.B: Restrain the arms tightly to stop the automatic movements
options.C: Ease the patient to the floor and clear nearby hazardous objects
options.D: Leave the room immediately to call the attending physician

explanation: Patient safety is job number one! Guiding them gently to the floor prevents nasty falls and bumps against furniture. You're going to be an amazing ward nurse! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h7)

question: How does positive pressure ventilation differ from how we normally breathe?

options.A: It relies entirely on cellular metabolism
options.B: It uses the diaphragm instead of external machinery
options.C: It pushes air into the lungs instead of creating negative pressure
options.D: It only removes carbon dioxide without giving oxygen

explanation: Think of normal breathing like pulling air in by expanding your chest (negative pressure). Machines or manual bags do the opposite—they gently push air right in!

question: Which body feature makes female patients more likely to get a catheter-related urinary tract infection?

options.A: A wider urethral opening
options.B: A larger bladder capacity than males
options.C: An absence of a muscular sphincter
options.D: A shorter urethra close to the anal opening

explanation: Spot on! The female urethra is quite short and sits very close to the anus, giving bacteria a short and easy path straight into the bladder.

question: A nurse wants to find the best evidence for managing pressure ulcers before updating the ward policy. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Throw away all current textbooks and rewrite the guidelines from memory
options.B: Formulate a clear clinical question and search a nursing database
options.C: Wait for a pharmaceutical company to mail a new brochure
options.D: Ask every patient on the ward what treatment they prefer

explanation: Evidence-based practice starts by defining the question and using an IR system to locate existing research. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T8#GNS113_U2_T8_h7)

question: In a mass casualty incident, what does a RED triage tag mean?

options.A: Minor injuries that can wait until the end of the shift
options.B: Immediate life-threatening injuries with a high chance of survival
options.C: Injuries so severe that survival is unlikely
options.D: Deceased patients who need no further attention

explanation: Spot on! Red means urgent. It tells us the patient has a life-threatening problem that we can fix right now to save their life.

question: What natural pain-relieving substance does the body release in large amounts during labour?

options.A: Growth hormone
options.B: Beta-endorphins
options.C: Antidiuretic hormone
options.D: Parathyroid hormone

explanation: The body is brilliantly designed! Beta-endorphins act as natural painkillers during labour by binding to special receptors in the nervous system.

question: What is the correct order for examining a patient's tummy (abdomen)?

options.A: Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
options.B: Palpation, percussion, auscultation, inspection
options.C: Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion
options.D: Percussion, palpation, inspection, auscultation

explanation: Always listen (auscultate) before you touch or press! Pressing first can change the natural bowel sounds and mess up your assessment.

question: When does the highest risk for postpartum hemorrhage and maternal death happen?

options.A: During the fourth month after delivery
options.B: Within the first 48 hours after childbirth
options.C: Two weeks before labor starts
options.D: At the final six-week checkup

explanation: That's right! The first 48 hours after birth are the most critical window for watching out for sudden, dangerous bleeding and infections.

question: What kind of items belong in the appendices of a research report?

options.A: The primary abstract and title page information
options.B: Bulky survey questionnaires, consent forms, and extra data tables
options.C: The main conclusions and nursing implications of the study
options.D: Personal opinions and reflections written by the lead researcher

explanation: Appendices keep your main text clean by holding large documents like questionnaires and extra charts out of the way.

question: Why do many pregnant women notice dark skin patches like the linea nigra on their belly?

options.A: The liver temporarily stops filtering waste pigments properly
options.B: Extra blood pools near the surface due to high progesterone
options.C: Sunlight exposure affects pregnant skin much faster than normal
options.D: Estrogen stimulates increased melanin production in the skin

explanation: Exactly! Surging estrogen wakes up the skin cells that make pigment (melanin), causing those familiar dark lines and patches during pregnancy.

question: Why is manual inventory tracking discouraged in busy hospital wards?

options.A: It uses too much electricity compared to digital systems
options.B: It makes medical equipment too heavy to push around
options.C: It stops doctors from writing paper prescriptions
options.D: It is prone to human error and wastes valuable nursing time

explanation: Manual counting takes nurses away from patient care and frequently results in unexpected stockouts. [learn more](GNS113_U4_T5#GNS113_U4_T5_h3)

question: How do smart beds help keep vulnerable hospital patients safe?

options.A: They automatically administer pain medication when turning
options.B: They replace the need for physical therapists on surgical wards
options.C: Built-in scales eliminate the need to chart daily fluid intake
options.D: Sensors alert staff when an unassisted patient tries to stand up

explanation: Brilliant! Smart bed exit alarms give you a quick heads-up so you can rush over and prevent a nasty fall.

question: What is the primary function of a hospital journal club?

options.A: To help nurses read, discuss, and understand research articles together
options.B: To discipline nurses who make mistakes during procedures
options.C: To write brand new research papers for international publishing
options.D: To raise money for buying new ward equipment

explanation: Brilliant! Journal clubs are cozy, supportive spaces where we break down studies together so everyone can learn without feeling intimidated.

question: A nurse tells a patient with diarrhea to wash their hands well after using the toilet. Which part of the chain of infection is this stopping?

options.A: Susceptible host
options.B: Mode of transmission
options.C: Reservoir
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: You're doing great! Handwashing washes germs away, stopping them from traveling to new surfaces or other people through contact.

question: Which IV fluid is the ONLY one safe to use alongside blood products?

options.A: Ringer's Lactate Solution
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 5% Dextrose in Water
options.D: Half-Normal Saline

explanation: Normal saline is isotonic and friendly to red blood cells, preventing them from bursting or clumping like other fluids might.

question: How is prevalence different from incidence?

options.A: Prevalence counts both old and new cases together
options.B: Prevalence is calculated without using a denominator
options.C: Prevalence only measures diseases that last one day
options.D: Prevalence ignores people who are currently receiving care

explanation: Think of prevalence as the big picture: it adds up all existing cases, while incidence only counts the fresh, new ones!

question: Which method do nurses usually use to gather health facts directly from a community?

options.A: Conducting home visits and community dialogues
options.B: Waiting for international health organizations to send reports
options.C: Consulting only with the federal minister of health
options.D: Reviewing international stock market trends

explanation: Great choice! Going directly into the community through visits and talks gives nurses a clear picture of real health conditions.

question: What is the difference between a felt need and a real need in community health?

options.A: A felt need is what the community asks for, while a real need is what data shows they lack
options.B: A felt need can be solved with money, while a real need requires federal approval
options.C: A felt need is written in hospital books, while a real need is spoken secretly
options.D: A felt need affects children, while a real need only affects elderly men

explanation: Communities often request things like a big hospital building, when data shows their actual greatest need is clean drinking water to stop cholera. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T6#GNS124_U3_T6_h5)

question: You just received a new delivery of canned milk for the clinic pantry. Where should you put the new cans?

options.A: On a separate table outside the storage room
options.B: In front of all the older cans for easy reach
options.C: In the refrigerator next to the fresh produce
options.D: Behind the older cans of milk already on the shelf

explanation: Always practice FIFO! Putting new stock behind older stock ensures the older items get used first before they spoil.

question: A patient on a hot day has been standing for hours at a parade and suddenly feels weak and collapses. What is the most likely trigger?

options.A: Peripheral blood pooling from heat and standing
options.B: A sudden increase in intracranial brain pressure
options.C: An acute blockage in the coronary arteries
options.D: An unrecognized epileptic seizure disorder

explanation: Heat and prolonged standing cause blood to pool in the legs, reducing return to the heart and triggering vasovagal fainting. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T16#GNS123_U3_T16_h3)

question: What is often the earliest sign that the brain isn't getting enough blood in a heart patient?

options.A: Inability to move the tongue
options.B: A sudden change in mental status or confusion
options.C: Yellow skin color
options.D: Pain in the big toe

explanation: The brain is a drama queen when it comes to oxygen—it complains immediately! Mild confusion or restlessness is usually the very first red flag that circulation is failing.

question: What makes a disaster different from a standard medical emergency?

options.A: An emergency never involves more than one healthcare provider.
options.B: An emergency only happens inside a hospital setting.
options.C: A disaster requires no coordination with outside agencies.
options.D: A disaster overwhelms local resources and involves mass casualties.

explanation: Spot on! While a normal emergency can be handled with the usual hospital staff and equipment, a disaster stretches everything past its breaking point because so many people are hurt at once.

question: Why is it better to test changes using small PDSA cycles instead of a massive hospital-wide overhaul?

options.A: It guarantees that every single change attempted will be successful on the first try.
options.B: It allows staff to test ideas safely, learn quickly, and minimize risk before wide adoption.
options.C: It prevents nurses from having to participate in unit meetings.
options.D: It completely eliminates the need to collect any patient data.

explanation: Smart thinking! Testing on a small scale keeps patients safe and lets you iron out any wrinkles without turning the whole hospital upside down.

question: What does 'horizontal equity' mean for patients?

options.A: All nurses must earn the exact same monthly salary
options.B: Hospitals must be built in straight lines across geographical zones
options.C: People with equal health needs must be treated equally
options.D: Wealthy individuals must pay for the healthcare of rural farmers

explanation: Horizontal equity means if two patients walk in with the exact same health problem, they get the same quality of care.

question: How does the schistosomiasis parasite usually get into the human body?

options.A: Skin penetration by cercariae in contaminated water
options.B: Inhalation of airborne dust near infected rivers
options.C: Ingestion of poorly cooked freshwater fish
options.D: Bites from infected mosquitoes near stagnant pools

explanation: The parasite doesn't wait to be swallowed—it swims right through healthy, unbroken skin when someone wades or swims in an infected stream. Keep up the great studying!

question: Why is low intervention fidelity a risk to a health program?

options.A: It automatically stops all funding from reaching the primary health centre
options.B: It makes community members refuse any future medical treatment
options.C: It can cause the program to fail to achieve its health goals even if completed
options.D: It forces the government to shut down the entire health district

explanation: If we skip steps or rush through procedures, the community won't get the full health benefits we promised them.

question: Why is 'system interoperability' such a big deal when hospitals share patient records?

options.A: It stops nurses from making any type of documentation error
options.B: It allows different health departments and facilities to share patient data smoothly
options.C: It ensures that all hospitals use the exact same brand of computer hardware
options.D: It prevents patients from viewing their own medical test results online

explanation: Exactly! Interoperability simply means different computer systems can talk to each other, so patient information travels safely between labs, clinics, and hospitals.

question: What indicates a successful outcome for a resident leaving a half-way house?

options.A: An inability to manage basic finances without supervision
options.B: The ability to maintain stability and live independently
options.C: The permanent loss of all contact with family members
options.D: A court order requiring them to return to hospital wards

explanation: You're doing great! Success means the resident can handle everyday life, look after their health, and thrive outside structured care.

question: Why does a high BMI raise a patient's risk for joint problems like osteoarthritis?

options.A: Extra weight places constant physical stress on weight-bearing joints
options.B: Fat tissue directly destroys cartilage cells
options.C: Obesity causes muscles to shrink completely
options.D: High body weight stops joint fluid from working

explanation: Carrying extra body weight puts constant pressure on weight-bearing joints like the knees and hips, wearing down cartilage over time.

question: What does the FIFO acronym stand for in food inventory management?

options.A: First-In, First-Out
options.B: Fast-Item, Fresh-Object
options.C: Fresh-Inspection, Final-Order
options.D: Freezer-Inside, Food-Out

explanation: FIFO means the items that arrived first are used first to prevent food from expiring on the shelf. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T012#GNS227_U3_T012_h7)

question: What usually happens when a nursing unit tries to roll out too many changes at the exact same time?

options.A: Initiative fatigue and staff burnout
options.B: A complete halt to patient admissions
options.C: Mandatory retirement for all nurses
options.D: Immediate financial bankruptcy

explanation: Too many changes at once can overwhelm anyone! It leads to exhaustion and makes it hard for everyone to keep up with new routines.

question: Which of the following describes colony morphology?

options.A: Measuring the exact temperature inside a laboratory incubator
options.B: Weighing a glass beaker before adding liquid nutrient broth
options.C: Observing the color and shape of a microbial colony on an agar plate
options.D: Counting the number of student desks in a microbiology classroom

explanation: Spot on! Colony morphology is simply looking at the physical traits of a bacterial colony, like its color, texture, and shape.

question: Which of these is NOT a serious warning sign covered by the ACHES mnemonic?

options.A: Severe pain and swelling in the lower leg
options.B: Mild morning nausea and mild breast tenderness
options.C: Severe chest pain and shortness of breath
options.D: Sudden severe headaches with visual disturbances

explanation: Mild nausea and tender breasts are normal, everyday side effects when starting hormones. ACHES is meant to catch the rare, serious red flags!

question: When managing an infectious disease, why should a community nurse look beyond just the individual patient?

options.A: Because individual treatments are rarely effective against infections
options.B: To comply with hospital administrative discharge policies
options.C: To prevent the illness from spreading to other members of the community
options.D: Because infectious agents only survive outside the human body

explanation: Great thinking! In community health, we treat the patient while also protecting the wider population from an outbreak.

question: Why is it important to test blood sugar while a patient is fasting?

options.A: It makes the red blood cells easier to see under a microscope.
options.B: It forces the pancreas to release all remaining insulin stores.
options.C: It prevents the patient from feeling dizzy during the blood draw.
options.D: It removes the temporary glucose spikes caused by recent eating.

explanation: Food intake naturally raises blood sugar temporarily, so fasting gives a clear baseline without dietary interference. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h1)

question: What is the name of the primary law protecting persons with disabilities in Nigeria?

options.A: The Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities Act
options.B: The Public Infrastructure and Welfare Decree
options.C: The Nigerian Social Services and Rehabilitation Law
options.D: The National Health Insurance Scheme Act

explanation: Passed in 2018, this Act protects the rights of individuals with disabilities and outlaws discrimination in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T16#GNS225_U5_T16_h2)

question: A patient is rushed to the clinic after a snakebite and receives ready-made antibodies. What type of immunity is this?

options.A: Innate immunity
options.B: Active immunity
options.C: Passive immunity
options.D: Natural immunity

explanation: Correct! Giving ready-made antibodies is passive immunity because the patient didn't have to manufacture them.

question: What is a common misconception about mental illness that fuels community stigma?

options.A: Knowing that counseling and medication help recovery
options.B: Believing it is caused by curses, witchcraft, or personal moral failure
options.C: Understanding it as a treatable medical condition affecting brain chemistry
options.D: Recognizing that stress can trigger episodes in anyone

explanation: False beliefs attributing mental illness to supernatural curses or weakness often lead to harsh discrimination and delay proper medical treatment. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T3#GNS314_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why is lactic acid so important during food fermentation?

options.A: It acts as a natural preservative by lowering pH
options.B: It adds a sweet flavor to the food item
options.C: It turns the food liquid before consumption
options.D: It speeds up the rate of food spoilage

explanation: Great job thinking about this! Lactic acid makes the environment too acidic for bad bacteria to survive, which naturally preserves the food.

question: Which of these action verbs should you avoid in a research objective because it is too vague?

options.A: To appreciate
options.B: To measure
options.C: To identify
options.D: To compare

explanation: Words like 'appreciate' or 'understand' are feelings—they are too subjective and impossible to measure accurately in a study. Stick to concrete verbs! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T9#GNS217_U3_T9_h6)

question: Why do we call vitamins and minerals 'micronutrients'?

options.A: They do not play any significant role in overall human metabolism
options.B: They are required by the body in much smaller quantities than macronutrients
options.C: They can only be manufactured synthetically inside a laboratory
options.D: They contain fewer chemical atoms than proteins and fats

explanation: Think 'micro' for tiny amounts! Even though we only need them in small quantities, they are still super important for our health.

question: If a category takes up 50 percent of your survey data, how many degrees should its slice be?

options.A: 180 degrees
options.B: 360 degrees
options.C: 45 degrees
options.D: 90 degrees

explanation: Well done! Since 50 percent is half, its slice has to be half of 360 degrees, which is 180 degrees.

question: Why does high national debt servicing negatively affect public health budgets?

options.A: It directly increases the number of patients seeking private insurance
options.B: It forces international health organizations to withdraw all nursing staff
options.C: It automatically lowers the market price of essential pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: It drains government revenue that could otherwise be allocated to social sectors like health

explanation: When a huge chunk of national income goes to paying off debts, less money is left in the purse for hospitals, schools, and health programs.

question: Which physical sign tells you right away that a patient is getting dehydrated?

options.A: Flushed and warm skin
options.B: Moist, pink mucous membranes
options.C: Dry, cracked mucous membranes
options.D: Bounding peripheral pulses

explanation: Dry mouth and lips are classic, quick red flags that the body is low on water. Always check the mucous membranes during your assessments!

question: A nurse manager creates a ward schedule that requires double the current nursing staff, ignoring the hospital budget. Which principle of planning was violated?

options.A: Continuity
options.B: Flexibility
options.C: Feasibility
options.D: Secrecy

explanation: Feasibility means a plan must be realistic and work within actual available resources like budgets and staff numbers. [learn more](GST321_U1_T5#GST321_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which leadership style involves making all decisions alone and giving direct orders?

options.A: Laissez-faire
options.B: Democratic
options.C: Autocratic
options.D: Servant

explanation: An autocratic leader keeps full control of decision-making and expects strict compliance from the nursing staff. [learn more](GST321_U3_T2#GST321_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which tiny flap of tissue stops food from accidentally entering your windpipe (trachea) when you swallow?

options.A: The vocal cords
options.B: The lower esophageal sphincter
options.C: The epiglottis
options.D: The soft palate

explanation: The epiglottis is like a clever trapdoor. It folds down over your larynx every time you swallow to make sure food safely slips into your esophagus instead of your lungs.

question: Why does cellular damage occur during prolonged shock?

options.A: Blood vessels expand and physically crush nearby organs
options.B: Cells lack oxygen to produce energy and waste builds up
options.C: Excess water floods the cells and causes them to burst
options.D: White blood cells mistakenly attack healthy body tissue

explanation: Without a steady supply of oxygen, cells cannot make normal energy, causing harmful waste products to accumulate and damage cellular structures. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h1)

question: What is a common reason why people strictly follow food taboos?

options.A: Direct orders from national medical boards
options.B: Lack of physical transport to farms
options.C: High market prices for the forbidden foods
options.D: Fear of social disapproval, curses, or bad luck

explanation: Taboos are tied to deep spiritual beliefs, so people worry about negative social or supernatural consequences if they break the rules.

question: What is the main purpose of the foramen ovale in a baby's heart before birth?

options.A: Connecting the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava to bypass the liver
options.B: Allowing blood to flow from the right atrium directly into the left atrium
options.C: Preventing maternal blood cells from entering the foetal heart chambers
options.D: Directing deoxygenated blood from the upper body back to the placenta

explanation: Spot on! The foramen ovale is a little flap-like door between the heart's upper chambers that lets oxygen-rich blood skip the right ventricle and lungs. You're doing brilliantly!

question: A nurse uses the hospital computer to check the medical chart of a famous musician admitted to a different ward, simply out of personal curiosity. What is the legal and ethical status of this action?

options.A: It is allowed if the nurse is off-duty during the chart review
options.B: It is acceptable as long as the nurse does not tell anyone else
options.C: It is a serious privacy breach because the nurse is outside the circle of care
options.D: It is encouraged so staff can offer collective words of encouragement

explanation: Looking at charts without a direct professional need for patient care violates data privacy laws and ethics. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T4#GNS113_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is a common complication when anxiety disorders are left untreated for many years?

options.A: Permanent loss of the ability to speak
options.B: Development of co-occurring depression and substance abuse
options.C: Complete immunity to all forms of psychological stress
options.D: Spontaneous cure of all medical health problems

explanation: Carrying heavy, unmanaged anxiety wears down a person's emotional strength over time, often opening the door to depression or unhealthy coping habits.

question: Which of these is a classic example of an environmental community risk?

options.A: A sudden outbreak of a viral infection
options.B: A high rate of unemployment among youths
options.C: Contaminated drinking water sources
options.D: Widespread cultural beliefs against vaccination

explanation: Bad water is a physical hazard right in the environment. It directly threatens everyone sharing that water source!

question: A patient handles ward stress by going for brisk walks and talking things through with a close friend. How would a nurse label this response?

options.A: Psychotic
options.B: Adaptive
options.C: Regressive
options.D: Maladaptive

explanation: Spot on! Exercising and leaning on a support system are classic healthy, adaptive ways to handle pressure.

question: How do routine clinic records generated from standing orders benefit the wider public health system?

options.A: They replace the need for community health educational campaigns
options.B: They guarantee that hospitals never run out of surgical equipment
options.C: They allow the federal government to tax private patent medicine vendors
options.D: They provide data that helps health authorities track disease trends and manage drug stocks

explanation: Aggregated clinic records show disease patterns, helping authorities monitor outbreaks and plan medical supply chains effectively. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is the key trait of a polyvalent nurse?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on surgical nursing care
options.B: Training across multiple clinical specialties
options.C: Specializing in pediatric medicine only
options.D: Working only in hospital management roles

explanation: Spot on! A polyvalent nurse is cross-trained in different fields, meaning they can comfortably move and work across various hospital departments.

question: Which of these is NOT a safe injection practice?

options.A: Reusing a disposable syringe after washing it with warm water
options.B: Disposing of used needles immediately into a puncture-proof box
options.C: Using a brand new, sterile syringe for every single patient
options.D: Wiping the rubber top of a medication vial with an alcohol swab

explanation: Never wash and reuse disposable syringes! Washing doesn't kill microscopic germs. Every patient deserves a fresh, sterile syringe.

question: What is the main purpose of holding an after-action review (AAR) after responding to a disaster?

options.A: To assign criminal blame and penalize individual nurses for minor errors
options.B: To analyze successes and failures in order to improve future disaster plans
options.C: To permanently close down the hospital's emergency department services
options.D: To calculate exact profit margins generated by emergency room admissions

explanation: An after-action review is never about pointing fingers. It is a supportive team chat to see what went right and how we can do even better next time.

question: A heart failure patient reports a sudden weight gain over two days during a tele-nursing call. What does this likely mean?

options.A: A healthy improvement in overall nutritional status
options.B: Normal muscle growth from starting a new exercise plan
options.C: Fluid retention that needs prompt medical evaluation
options.D: A broken weighing scale with no clinical relevance

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Rapid weight gain in heart failure usually points to dangerous fluid build-up that needs quick attention.

question: Which complication happens when high ventilator pressures cause tiny air sacs to rupture and air leaks into the chest cavity?

options.A: Pulmonary edema
options.B: Atelectasis
options.C: Pneumothorax
options.D: Pleural effusion

explanation: Too much pressure can pop overstretched alveoli, letting air leak into the space around the lung and causing it to collapse (a pneumothorax).
